passages.t: The desert blossoms, and Be strong, do not fear
passages.happening:
‘The wilderness and the land will be glad; the desert will rejoice and blossom like a rose’ (verse 1). It will bloom and rejoice with singing. The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, and the splendor of Carmel and Sharon. ‘They will see the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God’ (verse 2).

“Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!” (verse 3).

Say to those with anxious hearts, “Be strong, do not fear! Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 35 is the bright partner of chapter 34. There a land became a wilderness of thorns and wild creatures; here the wilderness becomes a garden and a road. Together the two chapters close the poetry of the book's first half.

The chapter's date belongs to the same debate as chapter 34. On the traditional view Isaiah wrote it in the eighth century BC, looking beyond the Assyrian crisis to a far greater restoration. Many critical scholars date it to the exile or after, since it seems to assume a people scattered far from Zion and shares much of its language with chapters 40 to 55; some suggest it was written to link the two halves of the book.

Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon were the most fertile and beautiful regions of the land. In 33:9 they withered in mourning. Here their glory is given to the desert.

Verse 4's vengeance is God coming to put things right for his people. The anxious are not scolded. They are told to take heart, because God is coming to save them.
passages.later: Hebrews takes up verse 3 for believers growing weary: ‘Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees’ (Hebrews 12:12). And chapter 40 opens with the same coming of God through the desert: ‘make a straight highway for our God in the desert’ (Isaiah 40:3).
passages.asks: The prophet is told to strengthen tired hands and say to anxious hearts, Be strong, do not fear. Ask whose hands near you are limp, and what you could say to them. And ask whether your own anxious heart can hear that God is coming to save.

passages.t: The blind will see, and the Way of Holiness
passages.happening:
‘Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped’ (verse 5). “Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy.” (verse 6). Water will gush in the wilderness and streams in the desert. The parched ground will become a pool, and where jackals lay there will be grass, reeds and papyrus (verse 7).

‘And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness’ (verse 8). The unclean will not travel it, and fools will not wander onto it. No lion or vicious beast will be there, ‘but the redeemed will walk upon it’ (verse 9).

‘So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Whatever its date, the chapter would have been heard by exiles who faced a long road home across real desert. The route from Babylon to Judah ran for hundreds of miles, usually following the Euphrates northwest before turning south, and the return that began after Cyrus's decree of 539 or 538 BC was hard and slow. A safe highway with water along it, and no lions, was exactly what such travelers needed.

The healing of the blind, deaf, lame and mute is a picture of God's coming kingdom, when everything broken is made whole. It is a promise about what God will do. It does not mean that anyone living with blindness, deafness or a disability today lacks faith or stands outside God's favor.

The last verse is repeated almost word for word later in the book. Sorrow and sighing flee, and joy overtakes the redeemed like a traveler catching up on the road.
passages.later: Isaiah repeats verse 10 in 51:11. And when John the Baptist asked whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus answered, ‘The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear’ (Matthew 11:5), in words drawn largely from Isaiah.
passages.asks: The redeemed walk home on a road where no lion can reach them, and sorrow and sighing flee. Ask what sorrow you long to see flee. And ask whether you are walking the Way of Holiness or wandering off it.
